utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Thursday, 7th of May, 2009. Good afternoon to Mr. Stojic, Mr. Petkovic and Mr. Pusic. Good afternoon, Mr. Praljak, who is testifying these days. Good afternoon to the Defence counsel, Mr. Stringer, and all his associates. Good afternoon to all the people assisting us. Regarding today's hearing, we'll first work until 4.00. We'll break then for 20 minutes, and we shall then resume until 6.00. Secondly, I have a brief ruling to deliver in private session, Mr. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Open session. Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just one other very brief thing, Mr. President. The Trial Chamber may notice over the next couple of weeks our case manager, Ms. Winner, will be absent from the courtroom because of a personal matter. Today we're joined by another of our very capable case managers, Mr. Sebastian van Hooydonk. I hope I've pronounced the name correctly. And he will be joining us not only today but on other occasions as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber welcomes you, case manager, as part of the Prosecution team. Our best wishes for efficient work, and I hope you'll help us work very well. Thank you. Mr. Kovacic, you may proceed. So far, I believe you have used something around four hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We are informed about the time. We keep track, with the help of the legal officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I suggest we go on. Yesterday, we saw one DVD where, among other things, there was a video of the attack of the JNA on Croatian coast towns, Sibenik, Zadar and Dubrovnik. You spoke earlier as well about the military danger to the Republic of Croatia, emanating from Bosnia and Herzegovina, where the JNA was strong and where it had moved its weapons; and inter alia Presiding Judge Antonetti asked whether and how it was possible to pass towards Split, whether it was possible for the JNA to get through to Split. Can you tell us about that? Was it possible, was it dangerous, and so on?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. Good afternoon, Your Honours. The honourable Judge Antonetti, in reaction to my clear statements that the former JNA units based around Mostar had already captured the areas around Stolac, Nevesinje, towards Dubrovnik, had the intention to create Greater Serbia, which was its general intent, I put forward one of the many books about that written by General Cokic. It's called "The beginning of the End." It's 3D03546, 3D03546. At the beginning, we see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mr. Praljak, could you indicate to the Chamber in which binder we can find the document because we have about six binders by now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Binder number 1. Before that is only an outline of Mr. Praljak's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So if I'm not wrong, first one is binder with statement of Mr. Praljak. And second one, I think that this one had number 2. That is the first one we need for this document. There is a list of documents on the beginning of the binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, the Trial Chamber has one binder containing Mr. Praljak's statement. Then we have three binders numbered 1, 2 and 3. Then we have smaller documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1, 2 and 3. This one is number 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I believe this is binder number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, while you're looking, I just would take the opportunity to remark that if this were a paperless tribunal, we'd all be looking at the document now. Thank you. And my thanks to the Praljak Defence, because the document is in e-court, and so no problems on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Stringer, you're right. But when we have documents of dozens of pages, you can't see all the pages in one go on the screen. If you have the paper document, you can really leaf through it, you know, have a quick glance at it all, and work better therefore. But you may be a whiz of the screen, you know. I grant you that readily.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So Jevrem Cokic was a general of the Yugoslav People's Army. The book is called "The Beginning of the End." It's 3D03546. The book was published, as we can see on the following page after the cover page, in 2008. And now I would kindly ask everyone to look at B/C/S page 12. That's 3D410614, paragraph 2. In this second paragraph, the general explains, from his own point of view, of course, the problems they were facing, the existence of right-oriented separatist forces aspiring towards secession and creation of their own armies, these forces forged territorial defences under their own command, and that all this worked to break the Yugoslav People's Army from within. He also says that the armed forces of Yugoslavia were composed of the army and the Territorial Defence, the latter being a republican regional force, and that this Territorial Defence was within the jurisdiction of republics and provinces. He also says that this created grave problems in command because there existed six republican, two provincial and one federal army; and all this was very complex and problematic. Then he says that in the mid-1980s, in a plan that I have already shown to this Court, the top military echelon adopted a plan called "Jedinstvo," "Unity," the essence of which was to restructure the entire organisation forces of the SFRY, and to this end the units of the JNA were made larger, military districts were established along the borders of the Greater Serbia, as it was designed, from the level of corps downwards, and these districts used to coincide with republican borders. And according to the plan, there were four theaters of war created. Let us now go to page 217 of the Serbian original. It says the military top echelon had the task to realise the plan of defence of the remaining Yugoslavia along the borders of the republics with majority Serbian population. The top military echelon had the task of implementing the defence of Yugoslavia, the rump Yugoslavia, that means without Slovenia and the part of Croatia that is west of the border Karlobag-Karlovac-Virovitica, on the line that coincided with the majority Serb population area. Nobody knows, of course, so what they considered to be the Serbian majority population. But he says in order to implement this, they proceeded from an evaluation of the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and especially of the prospects for the future. And, therefore, they planned regrouping of the existing forces in Dalmacija, in Herzegovina, and the bringing in of forces from the other areas. Preparations began for the implementation of defence of the remainder of Yugoslavia. The key areas -- the key territories were Dalmacija and Herzegovina. Towards the end of July, he was invited by General Blagoje Adzic, who was then chief of the General Staff of the JNA, and Blagoje Adzic brought him up to date and told him of the decision to form a group -- a task group for Dalmacija and Herzegovina. He was appointed commanding officer, commander. He was tasked to plan an operation urgently, to organise operation groups, and establish an operation group that was to carry out this operation in Dalmacija and Herzegovina, together with the Civilian Protection and Territorial Defence in that territory. On page 218, he continues this same story and says the command of the operation group, together with staff units, was to be set up to include commanding officers from inspectorates of the military forces, units of the 1st Military District located in the broader area of Sarajevo and a certain number of commanders from the General Staff of the JNA. And he goes on to say that all this was supposed to be done in a coordinated action with the Territorial Defence of the Dalmacijan-Herzegovinian territory, which was the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and on the part of the JNA the Knin Corps was to be involved. I would like to show where all this is on the map, if you can turn on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Usher, could you please be so kind to assist Mr. Praljak with ELMO. He brought a map to show those locations. [Interpretation] The Judges have the map, and it's always of assistance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Knin is here in Croatia. I'll mark it with 1 [marks]. So the Knin Corps was to be involved parts of the Sarajevo Corps - I'll mark it 2 [marks] - then the 37th Uzice Corps from the 1st Military District, Uzice is in Serbia; but I'm not going to look for it now, then the 2nd Titograd Corps, Titograd is in Montenegro, that's number 3 [marks]; and the naval district, which is practically this entire area here on the coast. He -- the author talks about how all this was to be done, because the situation was chaotic in Bosnia and Herzegovina, but he couldn't do anything about that, but the operation was a priority task. And he says that upon receiving and understanding this task, he conceived how to do it with basic forces from the areas of Herzegovina and the Knin Krajina, Herzegovina being here [marks], and the Knin Krajina, which is this [marks], and the naval forces from the sea who were to crush the forces in Dalmacija and link up with forces of Knin Krajina in Western Bosnia. He simply wanted, from this area of Knin [marks] and this area of Western Bosnia [marks], to crush Split, Sibenik, Zadar, and to emerge here [marks]. Due to the secrecy of this plan, only the commanders of the corps involved were let in on it. The commander of the 2nd Corps of Titograd, Mr. Radomir, Ratko Mladic from the Knin Corps, Major General Milan Torbica from the Uzice Corps - Milan Torbica is mentioned, as you'll remember, in orders to attack Mostar - and the commander of the Naval Sector Boka. This is Boka Kotorska, number 4 [marks], but the area covered by the naval authority was broader. And he says in stage 1, it was planned to use forces that are in touch with Croatia and the Knin Krajina, to continue offensive action, to capture Ravni Kotari. Ravni Kotari is here [marks], this entire area of hinterland of the Zadar. This is Ravni Kotari, so the plan was to take control of Ravni Kotari, "RK" [marks], to take control of Zadar and Sibenik, and to threaten Split from the west, to attack Split from the west. Parts of the operation group from the Kupres Plateau, which is going to be 7 on the map [marks], the Kupres Plateau, from that plateau they were to take control of the broader area of Livno - Livno is this, number 8 [marks] - to prevent the emergence and spreading of intra-ethnic conflicts in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the emergence of paramilitary units from Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. Of course, to talk about incidents caused by Croatian paramilitaries in Bosnia and Herzegovina is ridiculous, because we were barely able to defend what was left up here and all this was nonsense. He planned, upon completing this task, to continue the attack towards the broader area of Dubrovnik via Trebinje and to take control of areas such as Popovo Polje, which is here in the hinterland. Popovo Polje is here [marks]. The number will be 9 - towards the Adriatic coast to crush Ustasha forces and take control of Southern Dalmacija, and then go down the valley of Neretva to prevent further blockades by the JNA and the outbreak of inter-ethnic conflicts. So their idea was that everyone here were Ustashas, all the Croats and everyone that was not with them were Ustashas, and that was an excuse -- a pretext for mounting this operation. At the same time, they were to threaten the Adriatic thoroughfare to make traffic impossible. The first stage was supposed to be implemented within ten days, and then the second stage, the attack down the valley of the Neretva River[marks]. They had their positions on both the right and the east -- left bank of the Neretva. They were to go from this area of Mostar towards Split, and with part of their forces they were to attack from Drnis to Split [marks]. The task of these forces was with the support of the air force and the navy to take control of Dalmacija. The predicted duration was between 12 and 15 days, and that was the dead-line for completing these operations. I have nothing further to add. Can we have page 245 of the Serbian or, rather, 3D41-0618. Here he goes on to say that he had learned about the elements of the 37th Corps already being in the catchment areas. The 3rd Partisan Brigade was there and so on and so forth, the 37th Corps in Herzegovina. This is a poor photograph, but you can see columns of tanks moving. Your Honours, perhaps you will remember about when the people from Herzegovina stopped that tank brigade column heading towards the Kupres field with their bodies, that they were carrying tea there, and they were talking, and then Mr. Izetbegovic came and asked for the tank brigade to be allowed to pass through to the Kupres field. The column that was allowed to pass through was one of the main agents of this attack that was planned. Instinctively, of course, people knew that this would be the case. Nevertheless, politicians more often than not had little room for manoeuvre. I'm not saying that it was a bad thing, necessarily. But the people there knew that those tanks should not be allowed through, because it would soon blow up in their own faces. Page 246, the next one, 0619, he says that from the command post of the 37th Corps at Nevesinje, right here [marks] - Nevesinje is right next to Mostar. It's not marked on the map -- or, rather, it is. Here it is. That's Nevesinje, number 10. He ordered the command of the operative forces to start moving immediately. By midnight, the 20th of September, they were to reach the Ivkino Selo, Nevesinjsko Polje general area. We're talking about 1991 here. And so on and so forth. The next page, 247, the 3D number is the same, 41-0619, he says as units were being gathered in Herzegovina, at the same time in Serbian Montenegro there was a mobilisation progress of units that were supposed to then be joining the operative group. Members of the 37th Corps were located in the Nevesinje area and Mostar. The 2nd Corps was in the sectors of Stolac, Ljubinje, Trebinje, and Igalo. That is this barrier in East Herzegovina. And some elements of the 4th Corps were in the Mostar sector. The 9th Military Naval District had its units in the sea near the coast and the coast itself, and then air force support were at their permanent locations in the Neretva River valley, meaning the Mostar Airfield. That's where they were receiving support from. The last thing, page 352, 3D41-0620. Having received treatment at the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army, November of 1992, as chief of the General Staff, I found General Zivota Panic. I knew him to be a naval officer of a somewhat Bohemian disposition, but with leadership skills. He was appointed chief of the General Staff as a general who commanded the units of the JNA in Eastern Slavonia and Western Srem during operations conducted there, Eastern Slavonia here meaning Vukovar and the area around it. I will put in number 11 there [marks]. Did I mark that correctly or not? No. He goes on to say that this was certainly a very high recommendation for the position to which he was eventually appointed. So much for this book. I think the book is crystal clear, in terms of confirming everything that we have been discussing so far. All the documents point in that direction, as well as all the facts. I could bring up other books, should the Chamber so require. Could we please have a number for this map?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could we have a number for this one, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the map marked by the witness shall be given Exhibit IC1009. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. Your Honours, I was going to keep marking the map, as far as here. It doesn't look very pretty, but I think it's very clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The map that was used for this demonstration is 3D03545. It is the same map that you have, Your Honours, and we'll be using it whenever necessary?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: General, I would like to ask you a question about what you've just said. Right at the outset, you quoted the author. Every now and then, he talks about Dalmacija and Herzegovina. He sees this area as a single area. What about that detail? It's something that you mentioned. If you could please sum it up for us again. Is that in support of the theory that in a military sense, from a military perspective, this was a single theatre of war; the state borders were entirely irrelevant for this particular JNA operation?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I object to the leading question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Praljak actually said that, but I can rephrase. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, in addition to what you have been telling us about the JNA activities there and their plans, what else does that indicate to you, from a military perspective, in terms of state borders?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure how much point there would be in repeating this over and over again. He's very clear about this. We'll take whatever remains of Yugoslavia. It's not like he's having second thoughts about the republics or anything like that. What is at stake here for the JNA is that the plan to take the remaining areas and preserve Yugoslavia, as well as taking the Virovitica-Karlobag-Karlovac line, that was their objective, and there is not a single document to disprove that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: General, I know you understand that, but we have to do our best to make this clear to everyone in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But he says it two or three times, at least in the book, doesn't he?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Thank you very much. Unless the Chamber has further questions, I would like now to move on to my next topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have two technical questions to ask, because when you show a document, you can imagine that the Judges are going to scrutinise it, and on page 217, there are two matters which I've seen. This general of the JNA says this: He is speaking of paramilitary units, a few words, paramilitaries of Croatian paramilitary units. Could you tell us, in a few words, what are these paramilitary units, Croatian paramilitary units, in a few words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To him everything that had been done in Croatia to that point were paramilitary units. At the time in Croatia, given the fact that it was perfectly clear by this time that Croatia, not having yet declared its secession from Yugoslavia, could not have an army, true and proper; therefore, they pulled the reserve police forces up to that level to the extent possible at that moment. That's why I said yesterday that the first weapons that we could obtain legally were given to us by Hungary. We were allowed to buy weapons for the police, and then through legal channels, without violating any laws, we bought from Hungary 30.000 Kalashnikov automatic rifles and some ammunition to go with that. Another thing that was allowed was the establishment of the National Guards Corps, not an army proper. Those units numbered several thousand men. As a rule, when those units reached the lines along which the JNA had previously penetrated, they viewed all of us as paramilitary units. I was a paramilitary. We were all paramilitary. Any attempt to put up armed resistance was seen as a paramilitary attempt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... in 1991. Since 1945 - this is more than 40 years, roughly, nearly 40 years - this army, the popular Yugoslav, exists with all its elements, whether Serbs, Croatian, Muslim? You agree with me? And we know, and you said so, that several elements have established this. There are, in the structures of command sometimes, when number 1 is Croatia, number 2 may be Muslim, number 3 Serbian, and so on, or the reverse, conversely. Now, in this book he writes -- where he speaks of 1991, he qualifies the Croatians as Ustasha. How is this possible? How is it possible that this general calls the Croatians who are in the opposite camp of Ustasha? Do you have an explanation to give us? Well, for decades there was this army which was functioning, and because of dismantling of the country, immediately this word is being used. What is the explanation? Is it a sociological factor, psychological factor, or is it for propaganda? And you are a specialist, yourself, since you were chief of a department. For what reason is the word "Ustasha" used here on page 217 all the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, first of all, what you said about this commander and a deputy being a Croat, that's not right. That applied to political bodies, for example, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, but not to the army. Most of the men in the JNA, the greatest majority in all positions, were either Serbs or Montenegrins, in relation to the entire population. The share of the Muslims was substantially lower. I have used the statistics and shown it to you before, but I could do that again; next to no Muslims and even fewer Albanians. There was no way they could get promotion. For example, one of them was in the Croatia Army, General Ademi. Obviously, he was in the Croatian Army, but there is no way he could have made general in the JNA unless in pure theory. I'm not aware of a single Albanian who ever made it to the rank of general in the JNA. It was hard enough for the Croats, obviously. Back in 1991 -- let me say the following first. In 1991, people of the JNA came to the Croatian Army. The air force commander, Tus, he was air force commander in the JNA. Spegelj came too. There were two Serbs who crossed, for example, and many more, obviously, but I remember two; Sumanovac, who was General Agotic's commander, who was in charge of Croatian Army's air force. I'm not sure if General Imra Agotic is an ethnic Hungarian. I can't quite remember. And there was another Serb who defected. His name was Jezercic, and he crossed over to the Croatian Army. There was an ethnic Slovene, Gorinsek, who had been a JNA general. There were large numbers joining. At the time, he was saying something to the effect of, I'm not sure if two or three Croats should be in the JNA. Everyone had changed sides already and joined the Croatian Army. And now to the other question. I'll try to keep it as brief as I can. Ever since 1945, those Croats who even spoke out loud were immediately declared to be Ustashas. It was synonymous, at least for the purposes of Serb propaganda. If you spoke out publicly, somewhere in a public place, and said that you were a Croat, it was nearly equivalent to saying that you were a Ustasha. And there was this myth that was created about Jasenovac and the NDH, and this was something that was foisted on all Croats as some sort of collective guilt, with no end to it. It was impossible to live on under that pressure. I watched this happen for decades. And I will just tell you two things. For example, you needed a loan to build a road or a railway between Belgrade and Bar. Normally, this would amount to several million dollars. The investment was shared by Serbian Montenegro, say, and they bankrolled this together to keep the Croats from standing up against something like this. For months before, you would get a lot of propaganda about some Ustashas or some other. Needless to say, Croatia's political leadership had to calm things down and sweep the whole thing under the carpet and not say anything about it. Or this, for example: There was a large travel agency, Yugo-Tourist, Belgrade-based, and I followed that for about 20 years. They printed brochures. There was never a single brochure, never a single leaflet, not a single year that the word "Croatia" was mentioned. If you wanted to go to Croatia's coast, you would go either to Istria, or to Dalmacija, or to the Dubrovnik coastal area, but not to Croatia. In case you went any further south, you were headed for Montenegro's coast. Montenegro was a name that was used. So much for the history. It was very troublesome. All of us were branded as Ustashas en masse. General Tus, General Agotic, General Gorinsek, a Slovene, as soon as they joined the Croatian Army, they all of a sudden became Ustashas, and he branded his colleagues of yesteryear as Ustashas immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: General, the situation being what it was back in 1991, when the aggression began, there were, of course, some reactions abroad. You have told us about that, and no doubt you will more at a later stage. What was at the very outset the position of the US president concerning this entire situation? What was the position that they took in relation to everything that was going on?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see all this propaganda regarding Croats and all that. Even earlier on, it's not like this was something that began in 1945, after Ante Pavelic's regime, which was what it was, but it goes further back. Across the world, this propaganda gave rise to misgivings about Croatia. It simply wasn't something that you could avoid. To establish Croatia as a state was a work of art, simply because we were up against so much prejudice and reservation, the sort of thing that was being spread in those diplomatic statement circles ever since 1945. General Bobetko and General Tudjman, all of them had to defend themselves from this accusation. They were all partisans, but still they had no choice but to repeat the whole thing over again, that this was something that was not the case at all. It was very difficult to these ruts, these ways of thinking that were now deeply rooted. For some reason, they wanted Yugoslavia to remain. Croatia is a small country, and who cared about that anyway, especially given the fact that at the time all of this was going on, the great powers had more serious problems on their hands; the breakdown of the USSR, the reshuffle of NATO, no Warsaw Pact around anymore, the unification of Germany. Europe, as I was being told at the time by the French, the Germans, and all those who came, was this: Our war came at a very inconvenient time, because no one was free to look into our situation. There was no consistent foreign policy in this regard by the European community at the time. In this regard, we tried to repeat, over and over again, what are our principal positions were, how we wanted this state to exist and that we had no aspirations against anyone else, and also that the Serbs in Croatia, and you will be seeing that later on -- I will be showing documents, and this is something that is very important because this was something written in "Croatian Soldier" magazine which expressed our position at the time for Franjo Tudjman, Gojko Susak, some other general, myself. They were facts and so on and so forth. And there was a huge effort being made to disprove all this false information, unfounded information regarding our efforts, regarding our conclusions, regarding any agreements that we signed, and there you go, and so on and so forth. And here, there. When you read this later on to see what was reported, what I prepared here is several very short pages reflecting how the US president saw the entire situation. Bill Clinton, in his book "My Life," where as a matter of fact we see and where he tells us himself about all these basic problems and disagreements in the West about what to do in the area, especially given the fact that by this time there was the Gulf War already, and America was late jumping on this whole train. And when they finally joined the fray, they spoiled all the plans previously hatched by the French and the English. And when he wanted to join in, the French and the English tried to put a spoke in his wheel, the plans to resolve the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And then all of this had a dreadful effect on the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina, because people, generally speaking, and soldiers had certain expectations, thought that there would be an agreement that would be signed, and then that was that, the whole thing would be over. But when your expectations are let down, especially in the middle of a war, what you get as a result is that you have to keep climbing the ladder. And then there is another cease-fire that is signed, and a new plan comes along to sign. The Croats are the first to sign, and then suddenly everybody gets their hopes up, This must be the end now, we've reached an agreement. And this is again refused by Izetbegovic, more seldom, perhaps, Karadzic all the time, almost as a rule. And then the whole thing falls through again, comes to nothing, and then the chaos increases. But the saddest thing of all in this whole thing is that whenever these new proposals were tabled by the international community, conquests that had taken place up to that point in time were recognised as a fait accompli.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It might be a good idea, now that we've got the book in front of us, to hear about your position on the UN arms embargo. We might link that up to some topics that we'll be tackling later on, but perhaps you might want to tell us now. Clinton claims that the Americans at one point changed their position on that embargo imposed back in 1991.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, we'll tackle this briefly. At page 487, 3D330826, down towards the bottom of the page, and I'm skipping some paragraphs, he says, back in 1992, the European community recognised Bosnia as an independent state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Perhaps just to give the Chamber a hand, in the English it's 0839. The page in the book is 509, the right-hand column. Yes, it's right there.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the same -- it's 487, 3D33-0826.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, I got it right. It's got a different number in English.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In April, the European community recognised Bosnia. Okay. The first thing that has been perpetuated up to this very day, the name of the country is Bosnia-Herzegovina. The name is not Bosnia, it's Bosnia-Herzegovina. From the perspective of the great powers, obviously the same difference, Bosnia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, but everybody keeps saying "Bosnia." My position is that this has certain negative political implications as well. He says the first independence achieved by that country since the 15th century. That's quite right. In the meantime, Serb paramilitary units continued terrorising the Muslims and killing citizens. There you go. Not a single word about the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina again, and they were doing the same thing both to the Muslims and to the Croats. Then he goes on to say that Milosevic put on a show, pretending that he was withdrawing this soldiers from Bosnia, while he placed more supplies and more weapons under the command of Ratko Mladic, which of course is true. And then moving on to the next page, 488, that's a translation, 3D330827, talking about some economic sanctions that were meant to be imposed. At the beginning, there was resistance from the Secretary-General Boutros-Ghali, the French and English, who believed that Milosevic should be given a chance to stop the violence that he had triggered. Needless to say from the perspective of those of us who were there, this seems absurd, Milosevic being given a chance to stop the violence that he, himself, had triggered. It makes no sense at all. He triggered the violence with an objective in mind, and the only way to stop him from achieving his objective was for someone to tell him, Stop where you are, man, or else you get bombed. And then on from there, Clinton says that the problem with the embargo was the fact that the Serbs had sufficient weapons and ammunition to fight for years, to keep fighting for years. Therefore, the only real consequence of keeping the embargo in force was making it virtually impossible for the Bosnians to defend themselves. When he says "The Bosnians," he probably means the Muslims and the Croats. If he means that, then that's correct. What it should say is the Bosnians and the Herzegovinians. Then he says in 1999 we managed to push through, somehow we got the weapons, and then we suppressed the Serb forces, which is entirely untrue because no one could suppress or crush the Serb forces. All he says through small-scale supplies from Croatia that somehow slipped through the NATO blockade on the Croatian side. Well, that now is true, not small-scale supplies but, rather, maximum large supplies, the largest that could be achieved by Croatia under embargo. And then Mr. Clinton goes on to say that he proposes for this embargo -- for the arms embargo to be lifted, and then the Europeans were focusing on putting an end to the violence. The British prime minister wanted to force the Serbs to stop their siege of Bosnian cities, and they dispatched 8.000 soldiers to protect a convoy. Did they protect these convoys? Not well. To some extent, probably they did, but actual what this shows is no chance of me accusing anyone, I'm just stating a fact. The West -- the Western countries, for whatever reason, at no point in time really faced the facts on what was going on in Yugoslavia. And then for whatever reason, down towards the bottom of the page, Mr. Clinton says when he became president, and that was as far as I know, at the beginning of 1992, as always, the arms embargo and the European support for the Vance-Owen Plan weakened, weakened. It weakened the Muslim resistance against the Serbs. Even the evidence of the massacres against the Muslims and their rights was clear enough already. Now, one thing I don't understand. The European support for the Vance-Owen Plan, it never weakened, because in the next sentence Mr. Clinton says, In early February, I decided not to back the Vance-Owen Plan. It is my deepest conviction -- or, rather, based on what we knew, that was a total disaster, because the Americans now said, and I think that this is something that Lord Owen mentioned in his own book, and I think Mr. Karnavas also raised that, they were embittered because the Americans said, There you go, you and your plan. And then Clinton claims he met Brian Mulroney previously, Canada's prime minister, who told him he didn't like the plan. And then they completed a new plan for a new Bosnian policy, and Warren Christopher said that the US now will be joining the whole thing. Further on, he speaks about the road ahead, and he says that that road to a joint or unified policy is very long. "At the beginning of 1992, during our first meeting, French president Francois Mitterrand let me know that although he had dispatched 5.000 French troops as part of the humanitarian forces to prevent violence, that he was inclined to support the Serbs, and he was less inclined to see a united Bosnia under the Muslim leadership. I don't want to draw any conclusions." This is what it says, and this was written by the president of the United States of America, and there is nothing for me to add. And then he says, on the 26th of March, he's met with Kohl, and Kohl was inclined to support the lifting of the arms embargo. Kohl was inclined to support the lifting of the arms embargo. However, it continues by saying that Kohl and Clinton could not convince the British and the French of the same. They believed, in their turn, that the lifting of the embargo would prolong the war and jeopardise the UN troops on the ground. And now again I don't want to provide any comments. I just wish to say this: We can conclude, if we are going to draw any conclusion, that they expected for the Serbs to win very soon, and thus the war would end, or that they would conquer the part of the territory that they would be satisfied with and then they would stop. Otherwise, how could you have the third side without any arms and that the war could stop in that way? The only thing that could happen was for one side to kill everybody else on the other side, and then peace would arise. He says here that on the 26th, Izetbegovic met with Gore in the White House. Gore was the deputy president of the United States of America, and there was also the assistant for national security, and he was responsible for our failure to lift the embargo. Both Kohl and Mr. Clinton said to Izetbegovic that they were taking everything they could, for Europeans to take a firmer position in that regard. And after that, the Serbs were prevented from carrying out flights, which was not important at all. In April, Americans returned from Bosnia, requesting for military intervention. People who had been on the ground were very clear on that. They requested for a military intervention in order to prevent further slaughter. Further on, it says here they saw the killings, they saw ethnic cleansing on the ground. Elie Wiesel, a survivor of the holocaust, publicly requested from the president to do as much as he possibly could in order to stop violence. Up to the end of that month, the foreign policy team recommended that if the -- if the Serbs could not be convinced in any other way, the embargo for Muslims should be lifted. No mention of Croats there again, which is absolutely unclear to me. And so on and so forth. And it finally says after the first 100 days, we were still not close to a satisfactory solution to the crisis in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Britains and the French refused, the attempts of Warren Christopher, and reasserted their right to be -- to play the main role in dealing with the problem. On the ground, we knew that. We knew in our countries that there was a competition between the states who would reach a solution. This is a competition between the states from Europe and the United States of America in various combinations to see who would take credit for solving the situation. The matter of the fact was nobody was actually doing anything to solve the situation in any efficient way. Here, Mr. Clinton states that the tragedy would take two years to resolve and that there would be 250.000 dead, but this is not true. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, the number of dead on the three sides was around 98.000, of which 64 or 5 thousands were Muslims, Bosniaks. In percentage terms and in absolute terms, they had the highest number of victims. About 26.000 Serbs were killed, and around 8.000 Croats were killed, give or take a few. And now he says something that I believe is very important. Dick Holbrooke called something the largest collective security omission in the West from the 1930s, and this is something I have to deal with. I have to agree with him, unfortunately. All the facts were clear. Everything was very clear, who wanted what on what side. So, Your Honours, I believe we proposed that at the very beginning you could have dealt with the crisis in Yugoslavia in a very simple way. All it would have taken was to place NATO troops on the borders and say there would be no war, and, You in the country employ all the highest standards of democracy and deal with the problem. Croatia was eager to reach such a solution; however, without any success. And now what he says here is this: Holbrooke says an erroneous interpretation of the history of the Balkans. It was considered that the ethnic clash was too old and too deeply rooted for foreigners to get involved. However, this was not an ethnic conflict at all. Second of all, the obvious loss of strategic position of Yugoslavia after the Second World War -- I apologise, I'll repeat. So this is correct. Yugoslavia, which had been balancing between the East and the West and served as an example of a different Communist, although it was no different at all, but that's what the West wanted to convey as a message, when the Soviet Union broke up, Yugoslavia lost its strategic position. The victory of nationalism over democracy, as a dominant ideology of the post-Communist Yugoslavia, I can't agree with that, because no nationalism won over democracy. Democracy has its two parts, and the first part is introducing legal democratic standards; and then it takes years, for people who lived under the Communist rule, to learn how to apply democratic norms of behaviour. It takes a lot of time for people to learn that, and the best example is East Germany. East Germany, Prussia, and so on and so forth, before the beginning of the Second World War, were in very many ways much more developed than the western part of Germany. After having spent 40 years under the Communist rule, the psychology of that people changed radically. The Prussians, who had enjoyed a reputation of a very well-organised state, behaved the way they did, behaved as people would in socialism, and German sociologists concluded after that that people, Germans who lived in West Germany and those who lived in East Germany, that they would reach the same level of development once the children who went to East German nurseries died. And fourth of all, less willingness on the part of Bush's government --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I have a number of remarks. One is, in a way, procedural and helping the interpreters; and I would like to ask you again and ask everyone in the repertoire, including the Bench, that we should take into account that the interpreters are suffering a lot, because everybody speaks here without due attention to their work. It is my first remark. My second remark is that I really don't understand what is the relevance of, for example, the last items which you have taken as subject material, so how the Prussians behaved, et cetera, concerning our indictment. And we have talked about it yesterday. I do not want to waste time about it, but I would like to remind you and Mr. Kovacic which it is, indeed, our task to address the indictment and to talk about it, and of course to enhance your case which we are ready to listen to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, Judge Prandler is absolutely right. Our concern is the indictment, so please keep in mind throughout what you say what is stated in the indictment. I have not read the book written by Bill Clinton. I'm sorry I haven't, but I haven't, and it might be better somehow, because then I can remain absolutely neutral with respect to what you have just said. But I'm sure you have read the book, and since you are under oath, I absolutely trust the answer you're going to give me. In Clinton's book, and I -- and Judge Prandler just said it so rightly, I stick to the indictment. When he wrote this book, I suppose that he wrote the book surrounded by his advisers, people from the State Department, the CIA, the secret services, et cetera; so I suppose that he has good sources because when a former head of state writes a book, he can't afford to write any odd thing. So we can be -- we can believe that what he has written is serious, very serious, indeed. So based on this, does Mr. Clinton, in his book, mention three issues that concern me: The issue of the Greater Croatia? Does he say anywhere that Mr. Tudjman wanted to have a hostile take-over on Herzegovina in order to recreate the Banovina? Does he say so, expressly? Secondly, you spoke about ethnic cleansing, but I understood that you meant the Serbs in saying so, but does Clinton say anywhere that there was ethnic cleansing in Bosnia and Herzegovina because of the Croats in Herzegovina? Does he say so in his book? So these are my two main concerns, and I remind you that I don't know what is in the book, all the more so since I don't have the translations into English in the binder I received from Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for sometimes wandering, and I thank you for your warning. Let me say that nowhere in the book did I find that Mr. Clinton says that he heard Franjo Tudjman speak about a Greater Croatia. That's number 1. Second of all, I read the book, and I didn't see in the book that Mr. Clinton spoke about any sort of ethnic cleansing that would have been carried out by Croats in Herzegovina. What I wanted to demonstrate, on the basis of this book, is the following: The Western states were not unified, and it says here that in some European governments, they were not happy about having a Muslim state in the heart of the Balkans, because they feared it could be -- it could be turned into a base for the import of fundamentalism. What I wanted to show is this: War in Bosnia and Herzegovina was moderated by the discord among the states of the Western part of the world. One wanted one thing; the others wanted something else. And what I'm saying is this, Your Honours: The representatives on the ground followed their government's policies. That's how the English behaved, that's how the French behaved, that's how the Americans behaved. And they created additional chaos and additional confusion, and the whole thing made the war even longer and created a cause that in the indictment is actually ascribed to us, and I believe that's why this is relevant. And Clinton said in his book that he wanted to lift the embargo, and then he says, for example, I was against the decision to lift the arms embargo that was proposed by Senator Dole because I feared that would weaken the position of the United Nations. I also claim that after that, the American, as far as we learned in our contacts, that America weakened the embargo which stayed in place. However, the 6th American Fleet no longer controlled what was being transported across the Adriatic, and they also kept quiet when Turkish, Iranian, and other planes landed full of weapons. And let me not go on enumerating and accusing states. They would let all these things. The first plane from Iran that they had not approved, I suppose - this is a detail that is important - that was seized. However, they allowed us to destroy just one part of the weapons, because people on the ground had seen that what their governments were doing, in simple words, was not good; that one could not allow two peoples being killed without allowing them to get arms. For that reason, many officers and officials who served with the United Nations assisted us. The French did, the Spanish did, and they did it secretly, unbeknownst to their governments. They did it covertly. They couldn't do it in openly and publicly. They were not allowed to do that. However, they saw this as a good deed on their part. I wouldn't add anything to that. I would like to finish on that note. However, let me just say that Clinton says that he had made a confederation with the Washington Accord and he had forced Izetbegovic and Franjo Tudjman to adopt that federation of Muslims and Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that that federation would be part of a confederation with Croatia. To this day, I'm really not clear about this line of logic. And I'm just saying that this is how things happened, because if that part of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, consisting of Croats and Muslims, would have become part of a confederation with Croatia, then the Serbs would have entered into a confederation with Serbia, which would mean that there was no longer Bosnia-Herzegovina, or, rather --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, just one last question to go to the heart of the matter, because you can see that all my questions are now based and focused on essential things. Last question: There, where you're sitting today, several months ago we had the US ambassador in Zagreb. He came to testify. You heard it as well as I did, and I remember very vividly that he said that, Basically every day we'd go and see Mr. Tudjman. He would call him, but he was permanently, he said, close to Mr. Tudjman; for instance, also in November 1993, when the events occurred in Stupni Do. You, yourself, had positions of responsibility in the Croatian government because you were assistant minister, and then you joined the HVO, and then you went back to Zagreb as of the 9th of November, 1993. But in the various positions you held, did you feel that Mr. Tudjman's policy was under American control or that his policy was an absolutely independent policy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would sincerely thank you for this question, Your Honour. The policy of Franjo Tudjman was in his aspirations very clearly directed towards one goal. In order to reach that goal, under the circumstances of a complete -- and he always claimed, and he repeated and he parroted, and I'm not trying to insult the late president, that the Croatian state could not be organised if it was in discord with the international community, if there was no agreement with the international community, and that's why he always wanted to be in agreement. He wanted to be absolutely clear on what the West wanted. And the goal was for Croatia to be a democratic state, to be within the framework of borders prescribed by Badinter Commission. But look here, he had to obey, he had to listen, because those people didn't just come to have a chat. They said, You have to. If you don't, we will introduce an embargo, we will impose this and that and the other. We were too weak to talk at the equal footing with them. The ambassador of the United States of America was not a person with whom I could talk with as I would with my equal, regardless of what I thought of him, but he was a big person who was a representative of a big force. Franjo Tudjman could not tell Galbraith, I'm not going to see you today. He was not in a position to do that. And the second thing, Your Honours, it would have created a lot of confusion, and I know it fully well in some positions of Franjo Tudjman that were misquoted. Franjo Tudjman had two stories. One was real and pragmatic; he will do this and that and the other. And the second story was an attempt to explain, in historical terms; and they didn't want to listen to any of that, what would be the best thing for them to do in order to resolve the situation in the area. As historian with 20 or 30 years of experience before the war, he wrote his works, and he always repeated that we should do what the Scandinavian navy and states had done. He was somehow obsessed with the idea of a Scandinavian state and how they reached peace, and he believed that we should do the same, we should reach the peace in the same way. However, he never drew a clear line between his historical explanations and proposals as to how to best achieve the goal. And people who were listening to him misconstrued that, and that's why -- that's one of the reasons why they misunderstood him. An American does not have the time to listen to you talking about history. An American is here for 10 or 15 years as a company with a clear goal and a clear timeline.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Could I respectfully request that General Praljak speak a little bit slower. Sometimes it's difficult to keep track. It would be of some assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do try to slow down, Mr. Praljak. Yes, please continue, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I think there's no room for further questions on this. Could you just look at the screen from time to time, and then you will see how far behind the LiveNote is lagging. You do need to slow down. In this last portion, one of the main thesis is the existence of a variety of positions among big and powerful states on the developments in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the whole region, so the positions of the big powers were different. We just spoke about the Americans. How did the British look upon all this? Margaret Thatcher first condemned Milosevic; if it were not for him, there would be no war. Is it a simplification or did the British really understand the reasons for the war better?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to slow down. Just let me say one more thing about the Clinton book. He says, We did not really enforce the embargo on weapons because we knew that Bosnia could not survive. Weapons could not come through Croatia. Ms. Thatcher was no longer in British politics at the time. The her time was over by then. But she wrote a book which is called "Statecraft: Strategies for a Changing World," and of all the big leaders, she was the one who best understands what proceeded, what -- how the problems developed and emerged, who made a mistake where, and how it all happened. I could subscribe to everything said in that book. She put very clearly what it was all about. And as far as I am able to see -- again, you might ask what this has to do with the indictment, but I'd like to say a few things about the book. Look, for instance, at this lovely sentence. She speaks about the kind of policy where every national sentiment is labelled "nationalism." It's on page 15 of the introduction, 3D41-0098.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please indicate where it is on the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We can find perhaps the page if you give the number of the document first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D02642.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like your permission to cover a few topics that I believe are relevant to the indictment and are relevant to the case, but it's the break now; isn't it? Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters do not have the page on e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's 3D41-0098. Rare are those among us who are so indelicate to fail to notice --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Praljak repeat this or have this put on the ELMO or in e-court. We cannot do this like that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you look at the history of Croatia and see all the problems that Croatia had with other states, the moment the border with Hungary was established, the relationship between Hungary and Croatia became perfect. Page 25. That's 3D41-0098.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please indicate the paragraph on the page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sometimes fences have to be put up in order to have a good relationship with your neighbour. Our relationship with Hungary, with Italy, with Austria, were brilliant. All these were areas with which we used to have problems. Our relations with Serbia are improving, and they might even be good in some 15, 20 years, when certain issues are resolved. I'll skip all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It would be helpful also, when Mr. Praljak reads, to designate the paragraph so that the translators can follow along. And it might also be useful if counsel puts his headphones on so he can hear what exactly is being said in the booth. I don't mean to be directing around here, but someone has to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the future, when you prepare a document, Mr. Praljak, do endeavour to keep in mind that we need, of course, the page in B/C/S, but also the page in English, if you can, but in principle so that the English-speaking people can follow the text.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Page 224 in translation, English text, 3D41-0104. That's the English, paragraph 4. The heading is: "Criminal Courts for the former Yugoslavia and Rwanda." Paragraph 2 says: "The establishment of the Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia and Rwanda...." And so on and so forth: " ... constitute an act whereby the West and the broader international community admit defeat. In the former Yugoslavia, Slobodan Milosevic, and the main vehicles of his policy, had already used the Yugoslav People's Army and paramilitary gangs of Serb extremists to wage war against non-Serb population." Mind you, not Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina; non-Serb population: "Milosevic did this so barbarically and ruthlessly, in the plain view of the West, that Europe and the US could not have failed to see it. Moreover, on several occasions messages were sent that Belgrade interpreted as a green light for continuing these actions. After the greatest world's superpower, America, made a number of bad evaluations at the beginning of the 1999 conflict, and then persistently tried to apportion blame equally upon the victim and the aggressor, it had to find a way to respond to the increasing outrage throughout the world." Page 224, that's 3D33-0728, paragraph 1, one sentence that we studied in history: "Bismarck said on one occasion the whole of the Balkans is not worth the bones of one Pomeranian Grenadier." Many would agree with opinion of the iron chancellor. Unfortunately, that sort of thing was rampant in our war, but I would not agree with Bismarck on this. But the people who came to our country came with little brochures full of so many simplification and so much scorn and disdain that it was sickening to listen to. Page 245, that's 3D330729, the second paragraph in the middle: "The West finally did intervene in order to try to preserve the old Yugoslavia together, and exerted great pressure in public on those who are insolent enough to want to secede. Western states, among other things, imposed an embargo on the import of weapons, putting the aggressor in a far better position, and thus adding fuel to the aggression." A little further below, Baroness Thatcher says that the West mediated in numerous cease-fires, addressed numerous threats, and she thinks that it might have been better not to interfere in that way. It would have been better, in her opinion, to let us deal with it ourselves. On page 248 -- no, no, I can't do this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Just -- I've been quiet, and I'll continue to be quiet because it appears that the Trial Chamber, despite the admonitions to General Praljak to try to bring this testimony more closely to what's alleged in the indictment, the Trial Chamber is agreeable to his continuing, but just for the record, the Prosecution objects to this testimony as irrelevant. He's reading books of various individuals, politicians, the president, the prime minister, which is all sort of interesting, and maybe his point is that it's the international community that's responsible for the crimes that he's charged with. If that's his position, then let him say it. I mean, that seems to be where he's going. But it's our submission that this is irrelevant. I'm not going to object any more on this, because I think ultimately we get off track and we lose time, but that's the Prosecution position. This is irrelevant testimony. It's not linked to the crimes that are alleged in this indictment, which by the way doesn't include any crimes committed by any Serbs. But that's our position, and I'm just going to put that on the record for now and be quiet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You have produced resolutions of the Security Council, articles or stories from the British press. You have also produced several documents. So why don't you want an accused to be able also to produce some documents which come from political people of the United States, English, or other countries who are talking about these events? Why prohibit the accused to talk about this? But, Mr. Praljak, as for the book of Ms. Thatcher, which I haven't read - I think my colleagues haven't read it either - the only question, and I'm coming to the objective of my colleague Judge Prandler, and he's perfectly right, it is the indictment, and my question is very simple: Does Ms. Thatcher, in her book, speak again of the three subjects I talked to you about in the book of Mr. Clinton; a Great Croatia and the ethnic cleansing? Those are the subjects which are important. Does she speak or write about them, or as I got an impression, she only writes about the Serbs, the Serbians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Out of three things you mentioned, Ms. Thatcher did not ascribe a single one to Croatia or Mr. Tudjman. She speaks not only about the Serbs and the attitude of the West; she speaks about how the war started, how it developed, and about the conduct of the international community in all of that. You will allow that the indictment contains allegations about the joint criminal enterprise and our desire to carve up Bosnia and Herzegovina, and we read in Clinton's book that he brought Alija Izetbegovic and Milosevic to Washington to sign an agreement with Croatia, and that was a carving up of Bosnia and Herzegovina. After all I am not without intelligence and don’t tell me that I have committed war crimes before it has been proven in court. So, if it were just about, “Praljak, you have done it, and so on”, then all of this would be unnecessary. What we are talking about here is the effect of the embargo. Ms. Thatcher had a very good understanding of why things were happening the way they were happening. She understood the effect of the mass of Bosniaks expelled by Serbs, and the ethnic composition had been very balanced until then; and she understood how this fed the inter-ethnic conflict because disturbing the balance of ethnic population by expelling population and giving them abandoned apartments to occupy, that produces effects later on. These people do not care for anyone else. They are busy simply surviving. I think the conflict in Mostar and the conflict in Travnik, if there had been no peaceful ethnic occupation, meaning expulsions by Serbs, would perhaps have happened anyway, but it would have happened much later, on a much smaller scale and with much smaller effects. And it's very important to know this and very relevant to this indictment. I believe that lack of understanding of these things amounts to a logical fabrication and a legal fabrication. By presenting this book by Bill Clinton and the book by Ms. Thatcher, I wanted to show their thinking. And it's also important, in my mind, to know that the length of the war, as a particular variable on the actions of every individual, and on the moral stakes, will be the greater in proportion to the length of the war. The longer the war, you will have more and more individuals who will break down from killings, from starvation, attrition. These are important things. Or perhaps I don't understand anything. Of course, it is up to you Judges to see what you will do with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's time for the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Perhaps I can be helped after the break. If you look at page 42, lines 8 to 12, I must confess I completely fail to understand what Mr. Praljak tries to say here. Maybe it is lost in translation. So let's go into the break, and maybe afterwards it can be sorted out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We'll break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing starts again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, perhaps you could explain -- that is, clarify for Judge Trechsel what you meant on page 42, lines 8 and 9, where you said that the conflict in Mostar and Travnik, in the circumstances of these peaceful ethnic occupations of refugees caused by the Serbs -- something might have been omitted here. Could you explain?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. Your Honour Judge Trechsel, when I come to the paragraph of Ms. Thatcher that is relevant, I'll explain it very slowly and clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I need no paragraph at all. I want a re-translation or just what you have said between lines 8 and 12, because you speak there that the conflict could have been avoided, I think, or something, if there had been no peaceful ethnic occupation, and this seems very strange to me. I don't think that you wanted to say something like that. So if you can recall what you actually wanted to say, and say it slowly. Then the interpreters will translate that. It's a linguistic problem that I have.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. It's very simple. The waves of refugees, mostly Muslims that Serbs had expelled from their homes in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia, a large number of them went to Croatia and a large number of these refugees came to Central Bosnia. In that way, the ethnic balance between Muslims and Croats was upset, and that was an important factor that contributed to the open war that broke out in March 1993 between Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. This is very clear now. It makes sense, and I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me finish, Your Honour Judge Trechsel. What I just quoted is written by Ms. Thatcher on page 261 in the Croatian translation, and in English it's 3D33-0743, paragraph 3. I claim, once again, that the waves of refugees that upset the ethnic balance in Mostar and Central Bosnia were an important contributing factor in the conflict that broke out between Muslims and Croats, that is, between the BH Army and the Croat forces, because these people, in the general situation as it was, felt that they had no guarantee of ever being able to come back to their native areas. A huge number of them has still not returned, nor will they ever return. They were very embittered. They were people looking for a place to live, to inhabit, and neither in Mostar, nor anywhere else -- I'm not saying that the conflict would never have broken out, but even if they had broken out eventually, without this upsetting of the ethnic balance, the conflict would not have been so bad. And I believe that this was even done deliberately to provoke a conflict between Croats and Muslims. That was the purpose. I'd like to come back to page 250 now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, unfortunately I do not have the page you are reading from or you're looking at. There has been, indeed, a technical problem, but could you exactly say the sentence which was pronounced so that we'll have it on the transcript? It's probably only two or three lines. Could you please say exactly what she says on this question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll read it exactly. Page 261 in the Croatian translation. In English, it's 3D33-0743. I quote: "It is evaluated that 900.000 people sought refuge in neighbouring countries and in Western Europe, while 1.3 million were displaced within Bosnia itself. The burden of accommodating such a large number of people, especially in Croatia and Bosnia, was unbearable." Next paragraph: "Those waves of refugees brought about instability, and that was the purpose. The arrival of thousands of Muslim refugees in Central Bosnia, which upset the ethnic balance between Muslims and Croats, is an important factor that contributed to the open war which broke out between them in March 1993."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Mr. Praljak. In e-court, it's 3D33-0632, in English, and the page of the book is 301 in the English original, in the chapter "War Against Bosnia."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for having read this passage. The members of the Chamber appreciate it. Right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to go back now to the page 250 in Croatian. How come my numbers are different for English?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. Praljak, that's not English. That's for the Croatian version. It's the original page in the book and the e-court number for Croatian.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the first paragraph, Ms. Thatcher visited Vukovar in 1998 and says that everyone should at least once in their life face the material reality of evil, because when she saw Vukovar, she saw evil assuming a real face that no one can ever forget. She says that the area of Eastern Slavonia peacefully reintegrated into Croatia because Croatia gave up on any military action, and the United Nations scored its first success in peaceful reintegration, which was led by General Klein. And she says: "I also believed, as I had believed from the very start, in the summer of 1991, that Croatia, as a New Democratic state, needs all the support it can get, and that the support it had so far received from the West was almost negligible. Therefore, I accepted the invitation of the Croatian president, Dr. Franjo Tudjman, and the Croatian government to come for a long-postponed visit." And then in the next two paragraphs, she talks about the fact that Croatia belongs to Mediterranean Europe and that the rest of Croatia belongs to Central Europe. She says that Dubrovnik is a sublimely beautiful city and that the shelling of Dubrovnik was one of the stupidest tactical moves by Belgrade. She also says that the shelling of Dubrovnik --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Praljak. We really need -- do not need Maggie Thatcher to tell us that. This is completely redundant, because everyone knows it, and certainly the members on the Bench are very well aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] For the sake of the record and in order to facilitate reading, what Mr. Praljak has just read is on 3D33-0626. The original page is 288. The chapter is "Vukovar." There is a photograph there -- rather, the image of a map on that page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you have read from a part of this book. There may be another one you might have read, which I'm discovering now and which I will summarise quickly so that we save time. Apparently, two years before 1993, let's say in 1991, Ms. Thatcher had brought her support to Croatia and supported Croatia, and according to what she writes, she was going to be rewarded with a doctorate at the University of Zagreb. And there is also -- and because of that, she didn't go. So she cancelled her visit, and she says that those were attacks by Croatians, extremists of Croatia. Can you comment on this? Do you have anything to say about this? Because you used the book and also everything which is written in it, which is directly linked to the indictment. So this is what she's written. What can you say about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know about that, Your Honour. Ms. Thatcher was supposed to visit, but she cancelled the visit after what had occurred at Ahmici. Ahmici became a worldwide topic at the time. As far as I knew at the time, she believed that this was not a good time for her to be visiting Croatia, although we ended up wondering what Croatia had to do with Ahmici. Nevertheless, that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're not answering the other part of my question. Why does she speak about Croatian extremists? Do you have an answer? Because it's written here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand. Otherwise, I would have replied. It is not contentious, Your Honour, that there were groups of persons in Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is in relation to Ahmici. She is referring to extremists involved in that event. That is my understanding. It is a fact that the chaos of war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, there were, on both the Croat and Muslim sides, groups of people who were out of control and who were extreme and impossible to control, those who operated at night. In broad daylight, they would have formed part of the HVO, for example, but no one really knew what they were doing once they were back home from the front-line, with 15 or 20 days off to follow. Control was impossible under those conditions. Everyone, ranging from Franjo Tudjman to all the others, were saying, because this was a new democracy, and she refers to all these problems faced by new democracies, that it wasn't possible to lay the blame at the door of the leadership, be it Croatia's leadership or the HZ-HB's leadership, for not fighting hard enough to suppress that sort of thing. I clearly demonstrated that this is an arduous enough task even for states that are not at war, for full-fledged democracies. We were severely affected by this for the following reason: We ended up looking like we were to blame, and yet there was nothing at the time that we could do to eradicate things like that. To put it in the simplest of terms, it was powerlessness. A classic case of powerlessness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, I'll continue just very briefly. A couple of things remaining for us to see. The page is 259 of the Croatian translation, paragraph 2, and now you can tell me what the English reference would be. In this paragraph, Ms. Thatcher says that the Western leaders, faced with the threat, meaning Yugoslavia, committed three key errors: Firstly, they tried to preserve Yugoslavia, thereby making it known to the JNA that the foreign powers would not oppose their attempts to prevent secession. Secondly, the international community imposed an embargo, thereby making it impossible for Slovenes, Bosnians and Croats to defend themselves. And thirdly, quote, "in a bid to, 'in an unbiased fashion,' distribute the blame for these events," while in reality that was only one side - that was the aggressor - while the other side was the victim, the West became a kind of a co-culprit for the crimes that were committed. This was no, and I quote -- Ms. Thatcher quotes, rather, "fine hour "for Europe, as claimed at the time by the Luxembourg Foreign Minister Jacques Poos. Rather, this was the moment of European disgrace. In the last paragraph, she says a third of Croatian territory was occupied, roughly speaking, and I quote: "The UN forces were passive onlookers to the continuing ethnic cleansing of Croats from Croatia's territories. As Croatia's strength grew, they started to operate as the protectors of the Serb aggressor." Meanwhile, Milosevic and the military leadership, who had been allowed by international negotiators, without any difficulties being presented, to withdraw their heavy weaponry to Bosnia, were now able to set them to work against the non-Serb inhabitants there. Ms. Thatcher says: "What needed now doing? Number 1, when the constituent peoples expressed their desire to leave Yugoslavia, the attempt to preserve Yugoslavia at all costs was not permitted. Secondly, the side that was attacked had its right recognised." Number 3, one had to condemn the aggression against Slovenia and Croatia at its early stage, and place an ultimatum followed by military action. Air-strikes, combined with a supply of arms to the besieged, would undoubtedly saved Vukovar and other Croatian cities. Just to wrap this up, Your Honours, this is something that we and -- this war could have quite simply been stopped, nipped in the bud, quite efficiently. All one had to do was deploy along the borders, give us weapons to defend ourselves, and the Serb aggression would have been to no avail at all. This was simple. It would have proved efficient. Nothing is further from my mind than to accuse anyone at all, but the fact is, as is written here, this failure of the West to find its feet in this situation led to the results that we are looking at today. So that's that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Because pages 48, 49 and 50 were followed with a delay, the last bit read by General Praljak, that's from 3D33-0631. The next page, 0632, the pages would be 298 and 299 of Baroness Thatcher's book entitled "The Wars in the Balkan."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And just to add something that I forgot to say to Judge Trechsel before: The refugees and the very duration of the war, with all the expectations being let down, and this is something that has to do with the indictment, each month or every two months, there was an exponential growth in the numbers of people who were becoming morally decompensated.
