Throughout the war, the amount of chaos and the impossibility to exercise any form of control over the amount of problems that the war and the failure to find one's bearings, and the loss of any reference points, as far as the aid that was expected from the West was concerned, this goes to the very heart of the indictment. I assert that what is termed the political and military leadership of the HVO and I invested an endless effort; yet we were unable to overcome these problems. As for myself, I say, and I've managed to establish that, regardless of the daily amount of work that I put into it, which was never under 20 hours, regardless of my unquestionable courage, it was impossible to overcome the amount of chaos that was there. In that regard, I have to repeat this: If the indictment was already there and I was facing the same situation in the area, I don't know what else I could have done. I don't know what I could have done better. I did the best that I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General Praljak. If there are no questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a few follow-up questions on this document which I'm reading for the first time here. Therefore, I have questions to put straight off the cuff. First of all, I'll tell you how to read my questions. As a criminal judge, I tried to really look into depth and to have a clear overview of everything that is stated in an indictment, including what is in between the lines of an indictment. By way of an example, when a criminal law judge has to assess an air crash, he may say that there was a crash because there was a defect in the engine. Then the criminal judge will draw conclusions, make findings as to the cause. But if he is really thorough, he may find there was a defective engine, but when there was a breakdown, there was a light that lit up and pilots that were drunk did not factor that in. If they had, they could have corrected the situation. This is my approach, no matter what the field is. This is the way I work. I try to have a comprehensive overview of all problems. We've been here for three years, and I realise that the Serb element has to be taken into account when assessing the indictment. Ms. Thatcher says so in her book on page 302 in the English version. She says that while there was 31 percent of the population, they occupied 70 percent of the territory. This is a fact that cannot be ignored. But she goes further than that, so it seems, because she's a former prime minister of Britain; so what she says is probably better than what a journalist may say or than somebody who's just been on the ground for a few hours, because if she writes anything, she must rely on various sources. She wouldn't write anything. And her book is a very explicit criticism of the Vance-Owen Plan. She seems to say that there were consequences. One of the consequences is that the parties, be they Muslims, Croats or Serbs, wanted to take control of territory, which brought about, inevitably, conflicts, but she seems to put aside the Croats, at least in the pages that we have here. I don't have the entire book, but in these pages she speaks about Serbs, but she also speaks about Muslims, with the Mujahedin phenomenon. But curiously enough, I fail to find in these pages anything at all between the quote/unquote "the siege of Mostar." You have read the book. Does she anywhere in the book speak about Mostar? And if she doesn't, why doesn't she, in your view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I've read the book, yes. I'd just like to say this, a sentence in passing: The bibliography on that war runs into about a thousand books. I've read them myself and we have 28. We won't be referring to them all, needless to say. Why is that the case? I entirely agree with Ms. Thatcher when she says that when the plan fell through -- rather, look at it this way: The negotiators come to Geneva whenever they met, and the pressure is exerted on the weakest link, invariably, all the time. No principles were in force there. It wasn't a principle line of reasoning that was followed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll have an opportunity to revisit this. Just answer my question. Does she speak about Mostar or not? Why doesn't she? Because the "siege," and I always put it in quotation marks, of Mostar, she should have spoken about. Why doesn't she?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can only speculate. I don't know why she doesn't speak about Mostar, except perhaps she knows about what I'm telling you. The outbreak of clashes in Central Bosnia, in my opinion, and I have reason to assume that she had similar information at the time, was linked to the Mujahedin, the BH Army, and the ethnic dis-balance, because by this time they had understood that in international circles, those areas were recognised that were under some form of military control. As the BH Army didn't have the power to take back or reclaim the territories now held by the Serbs, it was only logical for them to turn to the Croats. For that reason, a theory was created here that several thousand or 8.000 people from Central Bosnia, from the HVO, attacked 2 Corps of the BH Army, and this borders on military insanity. This is something that I will use, books written by Muslim generals, to demonstrate to the Court beyond any doubt at all. And then they launched an operation towards the south, Mostar and as far as Ploce and Neum, and this is something that is written by the commander of the Muslim forces in his book. It's not something that Praljak is suggesting. It is then saying it in no uncertain terms. Had they won a victory there, they would have come to the negotiating table to say, All right, the West was well disposed to recognise and take for granted the solution that was already there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I infer from this that you do not have any specific explanation for this, so let's stop here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to state for the record, when you asked the general the question, he said, No, and then he continued his explanation. But he said, No, while you were still being interpreted, and that is off the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: General, let us try to speed things along a little, since we have lost a lot of time already. I don't think we should go into Richard Holbrooke --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or perhaps the three questions that we had in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, one speaker at a time, please. The interpretation is becoming exceedingly difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do not say that we have wasted a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we did not get your last remarks over the English channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I was asking Mr. Kovacic why he just said that we'd wasted a lot of time, but he has answered now. He said that he thought that we are just sort of lagging behind, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we should not start quoting Richard Holbrooke.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Maybe just something that we touched upon today. The Presiding Judge, His Honour Antonetti summed it up. What about Holbrooke, what about his entire book, not only the portion that we're using; any references at all to an alleged policy to create a Greater Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read Holbrooke's book "To End a War." I never came across any references like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Is it not his assertion in that book that the Croats, be it Croats from Bosnia, be it Croatia as a state, with its own army, were committing any acts of ethnic cleansing against the Muslims in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say specifically. I don't quite remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. Are there any references at all to the position that the Republic of Croatia was trying to annex parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, no references at all. That's the way I remember it right now. I've read a whole lot of books, but I would say no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's leave Holbrooke aside for the time being. We have now included the reference to him. The book is there. By virtue of his position at the time, he was in a position to provide relevant information. Anyone is free to go back to that, should they so wish. I think we should now move on to Dr. Alois Mock's book, edited by Herbert Vyitska. This was given to you separately, to the Registrar, because new numbers were assigned. Could that please be distributed to the Judges. No, no, I apologise. Only the general and I were given copies, and we have to give you the old page references for the transcript. I just wanted to simplify matters a little. The number in e-court will be 3D03552. In your binders, the numbers should be 3D0 -- or, rather, that remains, that's the e-court number now in your binders, it was 3D02649 and, in part, 3D03538. Mr. Praljak, can you get the new folder, look at what I'm --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll just try to be brief about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. My first question -- or, rather, what I wish to ask you first: Tell the Chamber why you think that the views of Dr. Mock are certainly relevant. That is the first thing that I would like you to explain. And, secondly, aren't Dr. Mock's positions essentially the same or do they not coincide with those of Baroness Thatcher?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read the book entitled "The Balkans in Croatia," written by Alois Mock. The then-foreign minister of Austria, was an outstanding connoisseur of the conditions in the former Yugoslavia, it's economy, it's politics, it's ethnic problems. He knew a lot about all these problems in their entirety. In the war, he played a very prominent role as moderator and particularly as someone who passed on the explanations to those further along in the West. He explained to everyone what warranted their attention. I assert that Dr. Alois Mock reached many conclusions that were similar to those reached by Ms. Thatcher there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you wish to point to any of his assertions that summarises positions of some relevance for Defence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would take us too far. I'm saying that he detects the same or similar problems as Ms. Thatcher in a very exhaustive way. I could go on talking about that for hours, but maybe that would not be welcomed by the honourable Trial Chamber. But what I'm saying is what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The next book that we would like to use is 3D03553. The author is Brendan Simms from -- and the title is "Britain and the Destruction of Bosnia." What is the main thesis in the book that prompted you to use this document as evidence and as one of the explanations of the situation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to the positions of Mr. Brendan Simms, the title is the best illustration, "The Unfinest Hour: Britain and the destruction of Bosnia."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, can you please quote number that is on the bottom as the page in e-court?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the title. 3D410230. I believe that the title page is the best illustration of everything that Mr. Simms writes in his book, "The Unfinest Hour," and it speaks about Britain and the destruction of Bosnia. If I were to try to show everything that is in the book, and the book is very long, written by a connoisseur, by someone who knew the situation very well, he speaks about the campaign of ethnic cleansing that fell upon Bosnian Muslims in North-West Bosnia. This is on page 7, at the very beginning of the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript, who is Mr. Simms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, I don't know. He is a politologist. He has offered some -- in any case, he is a political analyst.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The first thing that you wanted to draw our attention to is in the preface of the book?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is in the preface.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: This is 3D410785.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the preface, I'm reading from it now, it says, and I quote -- I quote half a sentence: "The Serbs have taken it as their goal to create an ethnically clean state from which they would eradicate every trace of the Muslim heritage." Further on, it says that they carried out ethnic cleansing, and I quote: "During the largest part of the year 1992 in Bosnia, there was no war. It was a slaughter, and Serb military circles, armed to the tooth and well organised, used their advantage against unprotected civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And so on and so forth. And then of course what is important here is this: He speaks about the behaviour of British military and political circles, and on the preface on page 9, he says as follows, and I quote: "Therefore, the most recent claim by Milosevic's Defence team in The Hague --"

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can you give us the page reference?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's page 9 in the preface. This is 3D410206.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have an observation. I don't know if it just regards the transcript, but the number given for this transcript on, sorry, page 58, line 6, is "3D03553." I have spent I don't know how many minutes trying to find this. It's a wrong number. It seems, at least in my binder, there are two numbers, 3D03100 and 3D03539. It would be very helpful if these numbers could be given carefully and correctly, because we lose time, and while we're looking for it we do not get everything the witness is saying. I have found it now, but it's an observation pro futuro.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Unfortunately, you're right, Your Honour. However, there has been some confusion, or people try to deal with yesterday's [indiscernible], which we were alerted. We tried to use some new technology and introduce everything together in e-court. The situation -- the very situation was not the best, and this is not good either, but everything was prepared even before that, so we have a problem at the moment and we can't deal with it, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand that there is some chaos even here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, I would like to quote from page 9 in the preface of the Croatian translation, and now you can give me the number for the English translation. Brendan Simms -- I'm going to say just a few things so that we don't lose much time with that. On page 9 of the preface --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. We can read the number now. This goes from 3D41/0785 to 3D41-0790 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I quote: "Through the Security Council of the United Nations in New York, and the NATO Consul in Brussels, for three long years the Brits resisted the use of air force by NATO. At the same time, British statesmen and diplomats were looking upon, in inverted commas, - strong – Serbia, as the best guarantor of peace in the Balkans. British mediators treated Serbs very amicably, and they were arrogant with Bosniaks at the same time. They used every possible way and mean to sabotage any American plans for a military intervention. Therefore, the most recent claim by Milosevic's Defence team in The Hague, according to which Lord Carrington and Owen had given him the green light," in inverted commas, " does not surprise at all." And then he says that this policy undermined the international reputation of Britain, and so on and so forth, or, and I quote from page 28 -- we are no longer dealing with the preface. We are dealing with something else. On page 28 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I may, this is in e-court 3D41-0790. Yes.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I quote the paragraph in the middle: "Of course, when you and commanders on the ground ask for a military intervention, British statesmen did not hasten to meet their demand. 'No cease-fire,' complained General Abdulrazek in December 1992. 'There is no progress. The situation is getting worse. All our efforts to save life and restore the basic services do not yield any results.' He demanded," the UN general, "to give a dead-line to Bosnia-Herzegovina under the threat of force. 'Guardian' wrote about a military operation. It is no longer possible to rest on one's laurels and say that this is being opposed by those on the ground. Nothing happened. There were no -- any advances, even when the French UN commander, General Cot, requested air-strikes in early 1994, after which he was immediately dismissed by the Secretary-General of the United Nations." And how did this look in propaganda terms? This is on page 29.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: This is the following page immediately after the one that we have just dealt with, thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And here Mr. Simms shows an example of a situation in which a girl, Irma Hadzimuratovic, had been hit by a Serb shell, and her mother was killed, and the girl was in a coma; and it says here her example was nothing out of the extraordinary. Numerous children suffered such wounds. However, thanks to the efforts of the BBC and the tabloid press, Irma's fate briefly became a national preoccupation in Britain. After swift intervention by the prime minister, the young girl was flown out of Bosnia, with maximum publicity and whilst disproportionate expense. I quote: "The aid agencies on the ground, who knew the British government's lamentable record on the evacuation of injured adults, were understandably contemptuous. Sjlvana Foa, the UNHCR spokeswoman, pointed out that Sarajevo was no supermarket for patients." And we quote her: "Does that mean that Britain wants only children? Maybe they want only blonde and blue-eyed children, maybe only children under the age of six."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Praljak, I'm lost again. This is an accusation against Great Britain, which may be justified and interesting, but I do not see any relation to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And it's something to which you have not been a witness, have you? Have you been there? Have you seen anything of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe I can add some clarity, maybe I can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was the objective of this and some other chapters, but I believe I can put my question now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: As you were reading the last part in this chapter, what did you actually want to convey, what message did you want to convey? What impression did you want to convey? What were the facts that had an influence on the conditions during the war?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to say the following: I quoted this not to accuse Great Britain. This was not my intention at all. However, the Croatian Defence Council and myself transported 10.000 wounded members of the BiH Army to Croatia, and this means at least 8.000 times some ambulance had to go to Split and further afield. We transported hundreds of wounded from the Mostar Hospital. The one, first, and then two helicopters that the HVO had at its disposal, I never managed to use it because it was always used to transport wounded, including wounded Muslims. There was a lot more publicity in Britain given to the transport of this one girl than anything that we might have done for over 10.000 people, and I am sitting here accused by a report when I was in Rama and in Uskoplje, when I transported a Muslim child suffering from leukemia, and its mother. And I was the one who brought over the TV crew to record what was being done because there were daily accusations against us. There were no facts to corroborate any of these accusations. There are no facts you can use to fight against such accusations if somebody is not going to accept a fact. You can do whatever you will. In keeping with this, in their reports about us, they he wrote the same things that were requested from them, from the British government, that they lied, they lied to everybody, and nowhere, in none of the reports, did they mention a reference to the existence of the Mujahedin in Central Bosnia. Your Honour Trechsel, that's by way of answering your question, and this is why I quoted a passage from this book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I don't think there's any more need to dwell upon this book.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If there are no further questions, I would like to move on to a completely new chapter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A question. Mr. Praljak, you have read this book, and you have seen that it uses a certain number of witnesses who came to bear witness here, in particular from the British Battalion. Some elements in the book come directly from the mouth of certain witnesses who came to bear witness here. This professor of Cambridge who wrote this book, tell us what you want -- I listened to you very carefully. What exactly do you want to show? Do you want to show that the British did not understand properly what was going on, and then you take issue with the very fact that they didn't understand the threat of the Mujahedin? What exactly are you trying to tell us by using this book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me put it in very simple terms, Your Honour. It is my deep conviction that the Britains, who are brilliant politicians and have been for centuries, knew exactly what was happening with the Mujahedin, because it would have been impossible not to understand. They were absolutely well aware of what was happening in Yugoslavia and during the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I claim that by following the policy of the British government and its political and military circles that is very precisely depicted here as a lamentable policy by Brendan Simms, I believe their people on the ground reported wrongly, erroneously, incorrectly, that they lied, and that their reports went in the direction in which this was suitable to the British policy, the policy of the British government, which was biased in favour of Serbs and which treated the Muslims and the HVO with arrogance. Incorrectly, arrogantly, their reports did not correspond to the truth; they did not reflect the truth. For example, if they saw three people from Croatia bearing the HVO insignia, they depicted them as an HVO brigade. They never wrote anything positive about us. I'm not saying that there were no people of that kind at all. However, the evidence is clear, the HVO, the HZ-HB, the overall structures, when they transport, with the resources that we had at our disposal at the time, when they transport 10.000 wounded of the BiH Army and everybody else, and nobody writes a single word -- a single positive word about you, how is that possible? You, Your Honours, listened to the testimonies by the representatives of the Spanish Battalion. Under my own leadership, on four occasions, we transported wounded from the east side of Mostar by helicopters, and except in their secret report, there's nowhere else a word about that in no newspapers or magazines. And that's how the situation was at the time, and in such a situation you could not demonstrate anything to these people, because they were looking through you and they were saying, We will write what we want, with -- and they treated you as aborigines or tribes. This was insulting. However, we were weak. If they invited you to a meeting, you would be insulted there. If you weren't -- if you didn't go, then you would go down as bad-mannered or ill-mannered, and so on and so forth. There was a meeting, and I'm telling you my own experience. The commander from Uskoplje asked to come to my office in Rama for a meeting, and I accepted that. He entered a room that was maybe six or seven square metres big, and he had a lower rank than me. He brought into that room his soldier with a cocked rifle. He sat down, and his soldier was there all the time with a cocked rifle. That was his attitude. Of course, I told him to go out, because I would not have been humiliated by anybody. I would not have sold my dignity, but this resulted in an argument. He asked me who was I, to not allow his soldier to stand there, and then I said I will bring four of my own, if that's what he wanted to do. That's what the attitude of these people was towards us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, you started off complaining about bad press from the English. Now you're speaking about a commander of Uskoplje, which if I recall correctly would also be called Gornji Vakuf. Was that a British -- was that a Brit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The commander of Uskoplje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Uskoplje, Vakuf, yes. I'm a Croat, and I call it "Uskoplje." It has two names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, but this commander, was it a commander of BritBat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, yes, yes, the commander. I don't know if it was BritBat or just one segment of a bat in that area. In any case, he was somebody, a major.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. That's an important point, because one could not see that it was a British person by reading the transcript. Perhaps you were a bit too fast. Okay, thank you for the explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript, on page 198 of the book, Colonel Bob Stewart wrote this: Several of his soldiers -- no, he's speaking about the soldiers, and he said some were professional servicemen, but they were all brave people. That's what Colonel Bob Stewart said about the commanders, about military commanders. We could spend hours on this book. Please proceed, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Now I would like to move on to a different topic, and that's the general's work in the Ministry of Defence in the Republic of Croatia. You, Your Honours, have that in your binder, as we call it here, and the title is "The Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we have an exhibit number, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Of what?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Counsel indicated that we're moving to a different topic, and he referred the Judges to the binder, The Ministry of Defence in the Republic of Croatia, and that suggested there was a new exhibit coming up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm merely assisting the Judges to find out first the binder, and then we go through the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which binder is it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please. Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The binder should have on the side the title "Croatian Ministry of Defence." Yes. [Interpretation] There are a lot of documents in this binder, of course, and unfortunately there is not enough time to look at all of them. It is our intention to just go briefly through some of the documents to allow the general to give an overview of his different activities while he worked in the Ministry of Defence. We want him to demonstrate that he did all sorts of things there. Somebody had to do those things, and at that moment it was him. As for the relevance with the indictment, in order to avoid some future questions, is the fact that the indictment alleges that Mr. Praljak was a permanent liaison between the Ministry of Defence and the HZ-HB or, rather, HVO; and if I can put it this way, he was in the Ministry of Defence of Croatia, he should have been sui Generi ambassador of the HVO or HZ-HB, and we would like to point out to some of the positions he held and jobs he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: First, General, could you please look at 3D00482. This should be at the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why did we skip the first two? I would like to go through them in my own order. Your Honours, can I read the numbers? Can I provide comments? It will take much less time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You can do that, but then we will not be able to deal with all that we have planned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, I mean, your lawyer is the one asking questions of you. He tells you what documents you are supposed to look at, and then you have to provide the answers. Please proceed, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We could take any of these documents. I simply tried to pick the most interesting ones. The first document in the binder is 3D00375.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Look at it, please, and explain, in a sentence or two, what the document represents.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 22nd of October, 1992, the American General Consulate -- just to say it briefly, the duty of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Please, General, just for the sake of the Croatian, the accurate name of IPD, what would that mean?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Information and Psychological Activity, which doesn't mean that it didn't deal with political topics, not just within the army. The IPD was a rather broad organisation. There was a section with psychologists who dealt with psychology across the units, and then all the units up to battalion level and even company level had their IPD men. One had to look after the wounded, the general condition of a unit, contact with journalists, providing all possible information to the journalists. Part of this was also the "Croatian Soldier," which was the magazine of the Defence Ministry. There was the brass band, and so on and so forth. In a way, anyone outside the ministry, when they needed something like, for example, a person shooting a movie, needing a tank for the movie, or someone tracking down new expressions, in terms of language used in the army, they would come to us for help. A broad range of people addressed us for assistance, this department which I headed until my departure. Among other things, here there is a lady from the American General Consulate requesting assistance for (redacted) to go to Zadar, Split and Ploce, to inspect that. By the way, (redacted) later on became a military attache, him being in charge of the humanitarian aid provided by the US, was obviously a perfectly normal cover used for someone who pursues other activities --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, one speaker at the time, please. We are no longer able to follow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Registrar, an order straight away. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So please refrain from mentioning the name and the --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. So that's what they're after. Needless to say, I seconded someone from my own department who was fluent in English and had university education, so in this other document, 3D00376, the gentleman, thanks for the exceptional assistance provided by the organisation, and so on and so forth. And by the way, no one ever came away unassisted, regardless of the country they came from. All possible forms of assistance were offered, in terms of travel, inspecting something or other. Whatever they were after, what they wanted to know, our positions, I'm under oath now and I'm telling you this, we were entirely open both in Croatia and in the HVO. All the journalists, all the TV crews, any organisation that approached us, they were free to go where they liked, for as long as they liked, in any way they liked, regardless of any military plans, forms of protection and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on, 3D00482.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 13th of January, 1993. The document has been mentioned before. Really, the representative delegation arrived from France. I won't enumerate them because the list is here. This is who came. They were met by General Tus and me. It's all there. Tus, of course --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right, General, let's leave Tus and what he's saying aside for the moment. I would like to draw your attention to the paragraph following Tus, on page 2 of the note. This is 3D19-0232, followed by page 234 and page 235. Those are the e-court references. Can you please tell them what you said in this conversation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's quite simple here. I told General Quesnot that the Serbs had promised their people a Greater Serbia. In this Greater Serbia or for the sake of this Greater Serbia, they were ready to give up on 20 percent of the territory, or even less than that, that they weren't interested in. Therefore, this whole story about Herzegovina seceding was something that emanated from Serbia's propaganda machinery; and I will use other documents to demonstrate that at a later stage. They proposed to the Croats to get Western Herzegovina in return for Krajina that would later be taken from them, and all the rest. Here, I go on to say that the Muslims were promised a common Muslim state. Alija Izetbegovic's positions were clear on that. Before the elections, he said either a civil state or a civil war. That's what he said, and documents will show that. I am saying here that they were in favour of a state. They had not prepared for war. They had suffered a lot of deaths during the ethnic cleansing, and now I know this first-hand from talking to Alija Izetbegovic, he simply -- for example, he did not wish to deblock Sarajevo--

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: There is something missing either in the transcript or in the interpretation. You said the Muslims suffered the most, the largest number of deaths… all right --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And then I say here that the Croatian position has been clear from the start.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Croatian position has been clear from the start, we are speaking of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The territory belonging to the Croats. Mind you, when we say "belonging to the Croats," the whole time we're saying things about this, it's not only to the Croats, belonging only to the Croats, but belonging to an administration over which the Croats -- all right, all the time we were talking about this from the beginning of the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Cutillero's plan. This state, the condition for the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina was that the state would be made up of three not pure ethnic -- no, no, no and no, but predominantly Croat. Of course, I'm not using the correct expression here, because that's what one said, belonging to the Croats, which stands for belonging to the territories that is predominantly Croat territory, which then overlaps with the borders of Banovina Croatia from the Kingdom of Yugoslavia; but not the Banovina that ended up belonging to Croatia, because this stems from the following explanation: The consistence with the 1981 census here -- I repeat, the Croats are in favour of an integral Bosnia- Herzegovina as a state, and they advocate the rights for Croats as a constituent people in that state. The problems between the Muslims and the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina are a result of the different aims of the political struggle. The Croats are fighting for a Bosnia-Herzegovina with autonomy for predominantly Croat-populated areas, so that's the point, and the Muslims are fighting for a civil state. What does this concept mean, a civil state? This is about a majorisation of the most powerful ethnic group. We were against a state that would be merely a civil state. You can't have a state that is not civil at the same time, but if it is only civil, then the group making up about 18 percent of the population cannot protect their own interests in any way at all. I then go on to say this --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The expression here is "civil state." We use a different expression here, a different term, which I think is better for our purposes. Do you remember the term that we used?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: United or unitarian state. When you say "in a multi-national state with constituent peoples," just civil, that means unitarian, because simply a greater number of civilians make decisions unable to protect a minority. In Croatia today, we have the protection of minorities rights, so they are elected directly to Parliament, regardless of whether there are 500 or 700 of them. Furthermore, and this is crystal clear when I say it, the Serbs are the common enemy. Good mutual relations, and the meaning here is between the Croats and the Muslims, get further apart or closer together depending on the activity of this common enemy. Your Honours, on the 13th of January, I mean, I believe that I precisely and without making any mistakes, say when our relations were based on the existence of a mutual enemy; but the fundamental problem of Bosnia and Herzegovina has not been resolved, and that was the internal political structure of that country. So what stems from this is the following: When the Serbs take the territory that they eventually took when they have been cited, there will be problems that arise between the Croats and the Muslims; A, because there is too little territory left. And then it goes on to say good mutual relations will be like that, depending on the activity of the common enemy. The Croats are better organised. They fought better. They started earlier on. They protected their own territory. The Muslims, at the outset, avoided any fighting at all. They simulated the status of refugees. They voluntarily became refugees, and they talked about an enormous number of units that belonged to them, but there were nowhere to be seen on the ground. And among the fighters, this created a huge psychological rift. In other words, on the one hand, you had a group with 17 percent, 2.7 times fewer than the Muslims, assumed upon itself the burden of the war. At the beginning, it was 90 percent, and then later on it still remained over 50 percent of the burden, and obviously the fighters were saying, Hey, hold on a minute, I hear them saying that they have 20.000 soldiers in this corps and that corps. I don't see them anywhere along the front-line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I go on to say that I'm convinced that 80 percent of the Muslims would accept a joint policy without any problems, as would all the Croats. And then I'm also saying what the honourable Judge asked, a problem is a large number of former JNA officers, who were Muslims who worked for their people

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did not work.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did not work, yes. Who did not work for their people -- no, no, of course I can't prove that, but you know I moved about a lot in the area, and one thing I can say is that a large number of officers from the JNA who came to the BH Army, well, a good number of them were working for the KOS, and they were working against the best interests of both the Muslims and the Croats. And when I get to that, when I start talking about Mahmuljan, I will show you how that works.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. There's one sentence -- one expression you have used, Mr. Praljak, that I would like you to comment upon. You say of the Muslims, on page 74, line 21-22: "They simulated the status of refugees." I find that a bit surprising, in that we have heard about large amounts of refugees, but the expression "simulated refugees" is something I would like you to explain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that is a misinterpretation. They didn't simulate anything, refugees or anything. They went abroad to become refugees, but they simulated units, units. In my book that I will present here, in his book Sefer Halilovic claims that he has an army of over 250.000 men. For God's sake, 250.000 men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You have answered my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you quite sufficient.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the other sentence uttered by counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The part that you were talking about, you're now finished; right? Okay, you're done with that. And then the last thing I would like to ask you about that document is page 4, the paragraph down towards the bottom of the page. You talk there or rather you given there -- or rather in that last paragraph here -- is this a faithful reflection of your position on UNPROFOR's role?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Briefly, please, no more than three sentences, what exactly were you trying to say?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The message here is that we -- or, rather, Croatia's leadership agreed to the presence of UNPROFOR. We wanted them there, and so on and so forth. All I'm saying is UNPROFOR is made up of the various contingents or elements. There were professional units involved who were doing a good job, and there were also those that weren't doing a good job. I'm not saying which ones, I'm not saying what I think, but there was a lot of smuggling going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: General, just a very brief question, please. You talk here about UNPROFOR in Croatia; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Another question about this. What about the late --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A quick last answer, because we're going to have to adjourn. Your last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thirty seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: General, what about later on in 1993? Again you came across UNPROFOR troops from different countries but the same organisation. Basically, did your criticism remain?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was the same criticism. [Indiscernible] zones, there you go. From the beginning of the cease-fire, we had 600 civilians who were killed and 500 soldiers, and they deployed right there in order to restore peace. They were great units, they were doing great jobs, professional units from certain countries, but there was a lot of drunkenness, alcoholism, prostitution, smuggling, all sorts of shady dealings going on. Again, not all of them. Most of them were professional, doing a great job. But they were just people, and that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have to stop, Mr. Kovacic. This week, you have used seven hours and twenty minutes. I think it was difficult to get going, but now I believe that General Praljak is aware of the Judges' concerns. We really want to be glued to the indictment. So whenever your lawyer asks a question, factor that in, and I think you'll be much more efficient. We'll run much more smoothly and much more quickly next week, and it will be 10 to 12 hours of your testimony. Well, you have the weekend to get ready, based on the remaining documents. You know what our objective is. We're listening to every word of yours, but it has to be relevant to your Defence case. In this way, the Judges can ask questions based on the documents, even though I initially was waiting towards the end of your testimony. But if I discover a document, if I see anything interesting in it, I do have to ask a follow-up question. So this is what I wanted to convey to you. I'm sure that it's going to get better all the time. I wish you a good evening. We shall reconvene on Monday at 2.15. We'll be working in the mornings next week, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 11th day of May, 2009, at 2.15 p.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
